input: In this passage, we are going to explore the pump affinity laws, which are a set of really useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is changed. There are three proportionalities that lie at the heart of these laws. First, the flow delivered by the pump is proportional to the speed, which means that if the speed goes up, the flow goes up in direct proportion. Second, the head produced by the pump is proportional to the speed squared, so a change in speed has a stronger effect on the head than it does on the flow. Third, the power taken by the pump is proportional to the speed cubed, which means that the power responds even more strongly to a change in speed than either the flow or the head. A simple worked check helps to bring this to life: if the speed is doubled, the speed cubed term means that the power is multiplied by 8. This shows just how sensitive the power consumption of a centrifugal pump is to the speed at which it is run, and why even modest changes in speed can have a noticeable effect on power.
target: The pump affinity laws give the performance of a centrifugal pump at a speed other than the speed at which it was measured. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the speed squared. Power is proportional to the speed cubed. Each law rescales the same pump: the flow, head, and power at the new speed come from the values at the measured speed and the ratio of the two speeds, with no other quantity entering. The worked check is the power law at a doubling of speed: the speed ratio cubed multiplies the power by 8. The laws are used wherever a measured pump is run at a changed speed, and their use is a substitution, not a new test: a performance measured at the original speed is carried to the new speed by the ratios, and the carried values stand in for a measurement at that speed. The proportionalities do not act independently in a running system, because the three quantities they rescale are the coordinates of a single operating point; applying the flow law and leaving the head at its measured value describes a point the pump does not pass through. Power is the quantity most exposed to a speed change, head next, and flow least, and that ordering is the practical content of the laws: a modest change in speed buys a modest change in flow at a disproportionate change in power. Any estimate of a speed change that applies one proportionality without the other two misstates the operating point.
